results.answer: A binary indexed tree stores at each index k the sum of the original array elements in the range [k‑p(k)+1, k], where p(k)=k & ‑k (the largest power of two dividing k) [1][4]. To compute a prefix sum sum(1,k) it repeatedly adds tree[k] to a running total and then moves to the next index k ← k ‑ (k & ‑k) until k = 0, visiting only O(log n) positions and thus running in O(log n) time [3].

A segment‑tree query only traverses a path up the tree’s height, and the tree has only O(log n) levels; at each step it moves to the next higher level, visiting at most a constant number of nodes per level. Hence the total number of visited nodes – and the work done – is O(log n)【4】【5】.

The union‑find structure determines that two elements are in the same set by finding each element’s representative and checking whether the representatives are identical (e.g., `same(a,b)` returns `find(a)==find(b)`)【4】【5】

The Z‑algorithm builds the Z‑array in a single left‑to‑right pass. It keeps a window [x, y] that is the rightmost segment of the string that is known to equal the prefix; for each new position k it first looks at the previously computed value z[k‑x]. If k + z[k‑x] < y, it can copy that value (z[k] = z[k‑x]); otherwise it must compare characters beyond y to extend the match and then update the window [x, y] accordingly. By using the stored Z‑values and only the necessary character‑by‑character comparisons, the whole array is filled in O(n) time [1][3].

Topological sorting yields a linear ordering of all the nodes of a directed acyclic graph such that whenever there is a path from node a to node b, node a appears earlier in the order than node b【1】. This ordering is a topological sort of the DAG【3】.

Yes. By precomputing a prefix‑sum (cumulative‑sum) array you can answer any repeated range‑sum query instantly (in O(1) time) by subtracting two stored prefix values; the binary indexed tree is introduced as a dynamic variant of that static prefix‑sum structure【1】【2】.

Jumping to the middle (as in binary search) repeatedly halves the portion of the list that still might contain the target, so the active region shrinks exponentially and the algorithm runs in O(log n) time. Walking through the list one element at a time examines each element sequentially, which requires O(n) steps, making it much slower for large lists. [2]

Compute a hash value for each piece of text (e.g., using polynomial hashing) and then compare the hash values; if the hashes are equal the strings are (with high probability) identical, while different hashes guarantee the strings differ【1】【2】. Because collisions are possible, you can reduce the risk by using multiple independent hash functions or carefully chosen constants【3】【5】.

Yes. An Eulerian path is a walk that traverses each edge of a graph exactly once, and it exists when all edges lie in a single connected component and either every vertex has even degree or exactly two vertices have odd degree (the odd‑degree vertices become the start and end of the path)【1】【2】.

Pick any node a in the tree, run a depth‑first (or breadth‑first) search to find the node b that is farthest from a. Then start a second search from b and find the node c that is farthest from b; the pair (b, c) are the two points whose distance is the tree’s diameter, i.e., the farthest apart points in the branching structure【2】. This two‑search method works because the longest path in a tree always has its endpoints at the farthest nodes discovered in this way【2】.

Keep a monotonic queue (deque) of the window’s elements. When the window moves, discard from the back any elements larger than the new entry, push the new entry, and pop the front if it has slid out of the window; the element at the front is always the current minimum, so you never recompute from scratch [3][1][4].

Amortized analysis looks at the total time spent by all operations in a sequence and spreads the cost of the occasional expensive operation over the many cheap ones, so the average (amortized) cost per operation remains low【1】【3】.

Picking the largest‑value coin first can be wrong for some coin systems; for example, with coins {1, 3, 4} and a target sum 6 the greedy choice gives 4 + 1 + 1, while the optimal solution is 3 + 3 [1]. The general way to obtain the minimum‑coin solution for any set of denominations is to use dynamic programming instead of the greedy rule [2].

A segment tree can be extended to answer many queries besides plain sums, such as minimum and maximum queries, greatest‑common‑divisor queries, and bit‑wise operations (AND, OR, XOR) on a range【1】. In general it supports “sum, minimum and maximum queries and many other queries” beyond simple range‑sum processing【2】.

Both binary indexed trees (Fenwick trees) and segment trees answer range queries and point updates in O(log n) time, but a BIT is a simple array‑based structure that efficiently supports only sum (prefix‑sum) queries and updates, using less memory and being easier to implement [1]. A segment tree is a binary tree that can handle many other associative queries (e.g., minimum, maximum) and also range updates via lazy propagation, though it requires more memory and is more complex to code [2][3]. Choose a BIT when you need only sum queries and want a lightweight solution; choose a segment tree when you need other query types or range‑update capabilities.
